rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Detailed criticism of Imruʾ al-Qays’s meter, grammar, and poetry falls outside this book’s purpose, so the author omits it.
rows.anchor: ثم رأينا هذا خارجا عن غرض كتابنا والكلام فيه يتصل بنقد الشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry follows an inherited, shared tradition; poets receive and use its resources according to their differing capacities.
rows.anchor: وإنما أردنا أن نبين الجملة التي بيناها لتعرف أن طريقة الشعر شريعة مورودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets may surpass predecessors, overlook meanings predecessors found, or share a meaning; poetic talent is distributed by God.
rows.anchor: والله يؤتي فضله من يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s composition and arrangement bewilder minds; the author promises to make its inimitability and supreme eloquence perceptible.
rows.anchor: فأما نهج القرآن ونظمه وتأليفه ورصفه فإن العقول تتيه في جهته وتحار في بحره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The science of Qurʾānic inimitability is noble and difficult, yet has few students and weak advocates.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا علم شريف المحل عظيم المكان قليل الطلاب ضعيف الأصحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even near-synonyms such as “morning” and “dawn” cannot be freely exchanged: one may fit a position where the other sounds misplaced.
rows.anchor: فإن إحدى اللفظتين قد تنفر في موضع وتزل عن مكان لا تزل عنه اللفظة الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human discourse may fail in comprehension, completeness, sound construction, wisdom, policy, or leadership; verbal and semantic excellence often come apart.
rows.anchor: ثم لو ظفرت بذلك كله رأيته ناقصا في وجه الحكمة أو مدخولا في باب السياسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān remains useful when expanded and complete when concise; sustained reflection uncovers successive beauties and inventions.
rows.anchor: وأنت لا تجد في جميع ما تلونا عليك إلا ما إذا بسط أفاد وإذا اختصر كمل في بابه وجاد

words: إن الملوك إذا دخلوا قرية أفسدوها
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the queen’s statement, each of the three clauses is brilliant, and the final clause is especially well placed and wise.
rows.anchor: هذه الكلمات الثلاث كل واحدة منها كالنجم في علوه ونوره وكالياقوت يتلألأ بين شذوره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s inimitable balance holds across short, medium, and long verses; readers should examine openings, endings, transitions, and joins.
rows.anchor: وهو تعادل هذا النظم في الإعجاز في مواقع الآيات القصيرة والطويلة والمتوسطة

words: إن فرعون علا في الأرض وجعل أهلها شيعا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concise account of Pharaoh’s oppression is offered as another passage for the reader to assess for Qurʾānic eloquence.
rows.anchor: إن فرعون علا في الأرض وجعل أهلها شيعا يستضعف طائفة منهم

words: وسيعلَم الذين ظلموا أي منقلب ينقلبون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing warning is an astonishingly apt ending; its force depends on its wording and on its fit with the preceding rhetorical pattern.
rows.anchor: الذين ظلموا أي منقلب ينقلبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of divine names and attributes in the opening of Ghāfir gathers noble meanings within an artful opening and close, unmatched in human speech.
rows.anchor: حم تنزيل الكتاب من الله العزيز العليم غافر الذنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the following verses, transitions between argument, threat, excuse, and warning unify varied subjects through elevated composition.
rows.anchor: ثم اتل ما بعدها من الآي واعرف وجه الخلوص من شيء إلى شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “to seize him” is uniquely forceful; replacing it with “kill,” “stone,” “banish,” or similar verbs would lose the passage’s originality and grandeur.
rows.anchor: وهل يسد مسده في الأصالة نكتة ولو وضع موضع ذلك ليقتلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited passage has four sections in its first verse and two in the next, whose arrangement contributes to its distinction.
rows.anchor: الآية الأولى أربعة فصول والثانية فصلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line naming Ḥamdawayh al-Aḥwal is ugly, heavy, and inept; the poet’s desire to digress obscures his judgment, though a graceful alternative was possible.
rows.anchor: ثم قوله حمدوية الأحول وحش جدا فما أمقت هذا البيت وأبغضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The horse-tail verse begins awkwardly and breaks the connection with what precedes; its contrivance fails to sustain the poem’s flow.
rows.anchor: فالبيت الأول وحش الابتداء منقطع عما سبق من الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase should have said “a tail like a robe”; omitting the comparison’s object leaves the connection uneven and inelegant.
rows.anchor: وكان يحتاج أن يقول ذنب كالرداء فقد حذف والوصل غير متسق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “As the robe is dragged” makes an awkward, inaccurate simile unless one supplies the unstated idea that the tail itself is dragged.
rows.anchor: ثم قوله كما سحب الرداء قبيح في تحقيق التشبيه وليس بواقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description “defending the rump” is neither apt nor truthful; the author contrasts it with Imruʾ al-Qays’s praised phrase about a tail above the ground.
rows.anchor: فويق الأرض ليس بأعزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison of the horse’s fetlocks to Orion is attractive but not original; poets commonly compared a horse’s blaze with the moon, stars, and similar images.
rows.anchor: تتوهم الجوزاء في أرساغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted twenty lines of horse description can be good or inventive, but remain within the shared practice of poets, among whom others equaled or surpassed him.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنا تركنا بقية كلامه في وصف الفرس لأنه ذكر عشرين بيتا في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other poets’ comparisons of the Pleiades equal or surpass the celebrated example, showing that this kind of poetic invention is common rather than unique.
rows.anchor: وفي جملة ما نقلناه ما يزيد على تشبيهه في الحسن أو يساويه أو يقاربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “appeared” is unnecessary in the Pleiades simile: the comparison works whether the constellation is high, rising, or setting.
rows.anchor: فقوله تعرضت من الكلام الذي يستغني عنه لأنه يشبه أثناء الوشاح بالثريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sash image is confused: the poet treats the Pleiades as one piece of a sash, then describes its plural middle sections; he meant a single piece.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن الثريا كقطعة من الوشاح المفصل فلا معنى تعرض لقوله أثناء الوشاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem’s sequence is poorly ordered: it mentions the encounter’s pleasure, timing, and guards before describing the woman’s state at his arrival; “by the curtain” is filler.
rows.anchor: انظر إلى البيت الثاني الأول والأبيات التي قبله كيف خلط في النظم وفرط في التأليف

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī explains “what recourse do you have?” to mean that the lover has no way to approach while people are around her.
rows.anchor: وأما البيت الثاني ففيه تعليق واختلال ذكر الأصمعي أن معنى قوله ما لك حيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Buḥturī’s first line strains for antithesis and uses more words than meanings; the idea itself is a commonplace.
rows.anchor: ألفاظه أوفر من معانيه وكلماته أكثر من فوائده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying simply “she is forbidden and forbidding” would express the point without the line’s verbosity and inflated phrasing.
rows.anchor: ولو قال هى ممنوعة مانعة كان ينوب عن تطويله وتكثيره الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparing a woman to the moon, branch, and dune is conventional and carries no special merit; arranging three comparisons is itself easy.
rows.anchor: وأما البيت الثاني فأنت تعلم أن التشبيه بالبدر والغصن والدعص أمر منقول متداول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualifiers that the branch is not bent and the dune does not cascade are strained additions; the comparisons already work without them.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله كالدعص غير مهيل لأنه إذا انهال خرج عن أن يكون مطلق التشبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Buḥturī’s line about beauty failing to please, “at you” is filler and the idea is common; moreover, it reverses the usual love-poetry claim that beauty inflames longing.
rows.anchor: قوله في البيت الأول عندك حشو وليس بواقع ولا بديع وفيه كلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kašājim’s alternative about beauty is safer and less flawed than al-Buḥturī’s formulation.
rows.anchor: وبيت كشاجم أسلم من هذا وأبعد من الخلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “in where” is awkward filler, unnatural to the speaker’s disposition, and mars the beauty of the verse like a leather patch on brocade.
rows.anchor: وأما البيت الثاني فإن قوله في حيث حشا قوله في كلامه ووقع ذلك مستنكرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s style remains consistent across varied structures, connections, openings, endings, and rhetorical paths.
rows.anchor: ونظم القرآن في مؤتلفه ومختلفه وفي فصله ووصله وافتتاحه واختتامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s consistency fulfills its own descriptions as free of contradiction, straight Arabic, mutually resembling, and clearly Arabic.
rows.anchor: قرآنا عربيا غير ذي عوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human speech changes tone and quality, mixing splendid and ugly wording, incongruous lines, and disordered composition; two poetic sayings illustrate such defects.
rows.anchor: وغيره من الكلام كثير التلون دائم التغير والتنكر يقف بك على بديع مستحسن ويعقبه بقبيح مستهجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hypothetical objection says some Qurʾānic passages do not display brilliance in individual words, but only in the overall passage.
rows.anchor: فإن قال قائل فقد نجد في آيات من القرآن ما يكون نظمه بخلاف ما وصفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list of forbidden relatives is necessarily a sequence of names, so its eloquence lies instead in its arrangement and the wisdom of its meaning.
rows.anchor: حرمت عليكم أمهاتكم وبناتكم وأخواتكم وعماتكم وخالاتكم

rows.speaker: قس بن ساعدة
rows.claim: The sermon attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida reflects on mortality, vanished peoples, changing fortune, and the return of what has passed.
rows.anchor: قال وهو قس بن ساعدة بن حذاق بن ذهل بن إياد بن نزار أول من آمن بالبعث

rows.speaker: أبو طالب
rows.claim: Abū Ṭālib’s marriage speech praises Muhammad’s lineage and virtues, notes his limited wealth, and offers to provide the requested bridal gift.
rows.anchor: & خطبه لأبي طالب &

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparing early sermons, reports, and eloquent speech with the Qurʾān lets readers recognize how Qurʾānic composition differs from all human discourse.
rows.anchor: ثم انظر بسكون طائر وخفض جناح وتفريغ لب وجمع عقل في ذلك فسيقع لك الفصل بين كلام الناس وبين كلام رب العالمين

rows.speaker: القائل
rows.claim: A possible objection says poetry surpasses sermons, letters, and ordinary conversation in eloquence and therefore seems the closest human comparison to the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: الشعر أفصح من الخطب وأبرع من الرسائل وأدق مسلكا من جميع أصناف المحاورات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse begins with mothers because they have the greatest inviolability, are directly related through birth, and are the nearest of the listed kin.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى انه بدأ بذكر الأم لعظم حرمتها وإدلائها بنفسها ومكان بعضيتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk kinship extends the mother’s status because milk nourishes the body and produces a relation comparable to partaking in the mother’s flesh.
rows.anchor: اللحم ينشره اللبن بما يغذوه فيتحصل بذلك أيضا لها حكم البعضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning milk sisters after milk mothers signals other relations derived through nursing and places sisters next to mothers in the sequence.
rows.anchor: وذكر الأخوات من الرضاعة فنبه بها على كل من يدلي بغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author leaves the verse’s full legal discussion to a projected book on Qurʾānic meanings, since that is outside this work’s scope.
rows.anchor: والكلام في إظهار حكم هذه الآية وفوائدها يطول ولم نضع كتابنا لهذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s legal wisdom compensates where inimitability cannot appear in individual words; its order and linked wording still display Qurʾānic eloquence.
rows.anchor: فلم تنفك هذه الآية من الحكم التي تخلف حكمة الإعجاز في النظم والتأليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names can make poetry effective or damage its meter and flow; Abu Dhuʾayb’s named-kin line is offered as an instance of successful placement.
rows.anchor: وقد يتفق في الشعر ذكر الأسامي فيحسن موقعه كقول أبي ذؤاب الأسدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Legal verses must use the terms their rulings require, yet whenever rhetorical freedom remains, the Qurʾān reaches unsurpassed eloquence through words, phrases, transitions, and endings.
rows.anchor: والآيات الأحكاميات التي لا بد فيها من أمر البلاغة يعتبر فيها من الألفاظ ما يعتبر في غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Careful readers recognize the Qurʾān’s distinctive mode and genre through the direction and endpoint of its discourse.
rows.anchor: بان عند أهل الصنعة تميز بابه وانفراد سبيله ولم يشك البليغ في انتمائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s composition does not vary or break down; it has the highest model and excellence.
rows.anchor: ونظم القرآن لا يتفاوت في شيء ولا يتباين في أمر ولا يختل في حال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hunting-and-food ruling combines wisdom, remarkable rhetorical movement, and concise choice, displaying inimitability even within one verse.
rows.anchor: أنت تجد في هذه الآية من الحكمة والتصرف العجيب والنظم البارع الغريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān handles legal material, including the commands in 7:157 and inheritance passages, with concise eloquence and an arrangement no human can match.
rows.anchor: أي بارع يقدر على جمع أحكام الفرائض في قدرها من الكلام ثم كيف يقدر على ما فيها من بديع النظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Passages of argument and monotheism, including the proof from the heavens and earth and declarations of divine unity, display the same inimitable composition.
rows.anchor: لو كان فيهما آلهة إلا الله لفسدتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath passage about the ranks, divine unity, and guarded heaven integrates successive claims and imagery into a single eloquent sequence.
rows.anchor: إن إلهكم لواحد رب السماوات والأرض وما بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doctrine of ṣarfa fails: if opponents were merely diverted from imitation, comparable pre-Islamic eloquence should exist among people who were never challenged or constrained.
rows.anchor: فلما لم يوجد في كلام من قبله مثله علم أن ما ادعاه القائل بالصرفة ظاهر البطلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Experts in eloquence recognize when speech can be matched; someone truly at the summit of eloquence would not presume to rival the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: ومن كان متناهيا في فصاحته لم يجز أن يطمع في مثل هذا القرآن بحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Claims by individuals that human speech can rival or exceed the Qurʾān do not settle the question; judgment belongs to eloquent people collectively.
rows.anchor: والمرجوع في هذا إلى جملة الفصحاء دون الآحاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents’ claim that the Qurʾān is human speech echoes the man who thought and plotted before calling it sorcery and human words.
rows.anchor: إنه فكر وقدر فقتل كيف قدر ثم قتل كيف قدر ثم نظر ثم عبس وبسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If imitation were possible but prevented only by divine diversion, the miracle would lie in the prevention rather than in any excellence intrinsic to the Qurʾānic discourse.
rows.anchor: ومما يبطل ما ذكروه من القول بالصرفة أنه لو كانت المعرضة ممكنة

rows.speaker: فريق منهم
rows.claim: Another faction says everyone could produce a counterpart if they learned the special method of arrangement; the author presents this as another claim that fails to explain the Qurʾān’s distinction.
rows.anchor: أن الكل قادرون على الإتيان بمثله وإنما يتأخرون عنه لعدم العلم بوجه ترتيب
